title: Nachiketa turns down the horses
hookLine: Death offers a boy horses, gold and a long life if he'll drop one question. he says keep them
carry: moksha isn't earned; it's what the self already is

cards: In the Katha Upanishad, a boy named Nachiketa watches his father give away old, worn-out cows at a great sacrifice. To whom will you give me? the boy asks, again and again, until his father snaps: to Death.
So Nachiketa goes to the house of Yama, Death himself, and waits three nights without food. Yama, who has left a guest unfed, offers him three wishes.
The third: when a person dies, some say they still are, some say they aren't. Teach me. Yama tries to change the subject.

Take sons and grandsons who live a hundred years, cattle, elephants, gold, horses, wide lands, as long a life as you like. Nachiketa says: these last only until tomorrow. Keep your horses; keep your songs.

teach.b: Shankara makes the same point in his comment on the Brahma Sutra's fourth line, which says, in effect: but that, because the texts are connected in it.
The small word but, he says, turns away an objection from the Mimamsa school, thinkers who take the Veda very seriously and hold that its sentences exist to tell people what to do.
So, they say, the Upanishads must be about action too. Shankara answers: no, they teach Brahman, something that already is. His reason echoes Nachiketa.
Anything produced by action has a beginning, and whatever begins also ends.
If freedom, moksha, were made by action, it would end too. So moksha isn't produced, reached, changed or cleaned up.
It's what the self already is, and knowing removes what hid it, the way a lamp shows a room it didn't build. Shankara isn't saying action is pointless; good action and devotion ready the mind.
But the last step isn't a doing. Some other Vedanta schools see freedom as the Lord's gift to devotion. Today it's easy to treat even the spiritual life like a points system.
Nachiketa waved the prizes away; this teaching says the deepest freedom was never a prize.

how: In Advaita Vedanta, good action and devotion are often understood as preparing the mind, while freedom itself is understood as coming through knowledge of the self.

o: knowing what already is, which frees
a meditation performed to make the mind calm
a ritual act that earns a place in heaven

games.q: Nachiketa and the fourth line — tap the pairs.

s: Nachiketa took Yama's horses and gold
he said they last only until tomorrow, and kept asking his question.
for Shankara, freedom is the product of the right action
whatever action produces has a beginning and so an end. freedom, he says, is eternal.
for Shankara, good action and devotion can ready the mind
they prepare the ground; the last step is knowing what already is.

games.q: a Mimamsa thinker says: the Veda tells people what to do, so the Upanishads must be about action too. you're Shankara. what do you answer?
o: agreed: freedom is the reward for the right ritual.
no: they teach what already is, and freedom isn't made.
the Upanishads aren't part of the Veda.
games.why: Shankara says anything made by action ends, so freedom, which is eternal, comes by knowing, not doing.

practice: Bring to mind two or three things you'll do today. As each one comes up, offer it in your heart without asking what it will earn; many Hindus do this with a short prayer, or at the family altar in the morning.
Then, for a few breaths, stop adding effort, and notice what's already here without making anything. If you don't pray, simply let the reward go.

wordCard.voice: Jnana. Knowing. On the fourth line, Shankara says freedom isn't produced by any action, so what frees is knowing what already is.

orig.note: Sanskrit: connection, harmony; the key word of Brahma Sutra 1.1.4, the texts fitting together in Brahman.

carryVoice: Your line: moksha isn't earned; it's what the self already is. Keep your horses, said the boy. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Katha Upanishad 1.1.1–1.1.29 (Nachiketa's father gives away worn-out cows; 'to Death I give you'; three nights unfed in Yama's house; three boons; Yama's offers of long-lived sons, cattle, elephants, gold, horses, land and long life; 'these last until tomorrow; keep your horses, dance and song')
Katha Upanishad 1.2.1–1.2.4 (the good, shreyas, and the pleasant, preyas, both approach a person; the wise choose the good; Yama praises Nachiketa for not being tempted)
Brahma Sutra 1.1.4 (but that, because of connection)

Shankara, Brahma Sutra Bhashya 1.1.4 ('but' sets aside the objection; the Mimamsa view that Vedic sentences aim at action; the Upanishads teach an existing Brahman; what is produced is non-eternal; release is not produced, reached, modified or purified; knowledge removes the obstacle)
